name: Denosumab
className: Monoclonal antibody (RANKL inhibitor) for bone disease

formulations.label: Solution for injection in pre-filled syringe (60 mg)
formulations.note: This is the 60 mg (osteoporosis) product. A separate 120 mg denosumab product for cancer indications has different contraindications and is not covered here.

src.q: Each pre-filled syringe contains 60 mg of denosumab in 1 mL of solution (60 mg/mL).
The contraindications vary between the 2 doses, because their indications are different.

bnf.note: BNF/BNFC is only available in the UK; not accessed.

items.t: Osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and in men at increased risk of fracture; bone loss with hormone ablation in men with prostate cancer at increased fracture risk; bone loss with long-term systemic glucocorticoid therapy in adults at increased fracture risk.

src.q: Treatment of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and in men at increased risk of fractures.
Treatment of bone loss associated with hormone ablation in men with prostate cancer at increased risk of fractures
Treatment of bone loss associated with long-term systemic glucocorticoid therapy in adult patients at increased risk of fracture

items.t: MHRA: patients should not stop denosumab without specialist review (risk of multiple vertebral fractures after stopping or delaying).

src.q: patients should not stop denosumab without specialist review

items.t: Biological medicine: record the product name and batch number.

src.q: In order to improve the traceability of biological medicinal products, the name and the batch number of the administered product should be clearly recorded.

items.t: 60 mg by subcutaneous injection once every 6 months (thigh, abdomen or upper arm). Patients must have adequate calcium and vitamin D.

src.q: The recommended dose is 60 mg denosumab administered as a single subcutaneous injection once every 6 months into the thigh, abdomen or upper arm.
Patients must be adequately supplemented with calcium and vitamin D

items.t: Optimal treatment length not established; re-evaluate periodically, especially after 5 or more years.

src.q: The need for continued treatment should be re-evaluated periodically based on the benefits and potential risks of denosumab on an individual patient basis, particularly after 5 or more years of use

items.t: MHRA: if a dose is missed, give it as soon as possible, then schedule the next injection 6 months from that date.

src.q: if you miss a prescribed dose of denosumab, the missed injection should be administered as soon as possible. After this, your next injection will be scheduled 6 months from the date of your last injection

items.t: Elderly: no dose adjustment.

src.q: No dose adjustment is required in elderly patients.

items.t: Should not be used under 18 years: serious hypercalcaemia (some with acute kidney injury), possible inhibition of bone growth and tooth eruption. MHRA confirms: adults (18 and over) only.

src.q: Prolia should not be used in children aged < 18 years because of safety concerns of serious hypercalcaemia, and potential inhibition of bone growth and lack of tooth eruption
denosumab 60mg (Prolia) should not be used in children and adolescents younger than 18 years

items.t: Hypersensitivity to denosumab or excipients; hypocalcaemia.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1. Hypocalcaemia

items.t: Hypocalcaemia: correct before starting. Severe symptomatic (including fatal) cases reported, mostly in the first weeks but also later. Concomitant glucocorticoids add to the risk.

src.q: Hypocalcaemia must be corrected by adequate intake of calcium and vitamin D before initiating therapy.
severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia (resulting in hospitalisation, life-threatening events, and fatal cases) has been reported
Concomitant glucocorticoid treatment is an additional risk factor for hypocalcaemia.

items.t: Severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min) or dialysis: greater risk of hypocalcaemia and PTH rise; severe and fatal cases. Calcium, vitamin D and regular calcium monitoring are especially important.

src.q: Patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance < 30 mL/min) or receiving dialysis are at greater risk of developing hypocalcaemia.
Adequate intake of calcium, vitamin D and regular monitoring of calcium is especially important in these patients

items.t: Stopping treatment: bone density falls and fracture risk rises. MHRA: multiple vertebral fractures within 18 months of stopping or delaying; highest risk with previous vertebral fracture. Monitor BMD and consider alternative treatment.

src.q: Following denosumab discontinuation, decrease in bone mineral density (BMD) is expected (see section 5.1), leading to an increased risk for fractures.
an increased risk of multiple vertebral fractures has been reported in patients within 18 months of stopping or delaying ongoing denosumab 60mg treatment for osteoporosis
patients with a previous vertebral fracture may be at highest risk

items.t: Osteonecrosis of the jaw: delay starting with unhealed open mouth lesions; dental check and preventive dentistry if risk factors. Avoid invasive dental procedures close to a dose.

src.q: The start of treatment/new treatment course should be delayed in patients with unhealed open soft tissue lesions in the mouth.
invasive dental procedures should be performed only after careful consideration and be avoided in close proximity to denosumab administration

items.t: Atypical femoral fractures: ask about new thigh, hip or groin pain; examine the other femur after a femoral shaft fracture. Osteonecrosis of the external auditory canal also reported.

src.q: During denosumab treatment, patients should be advised to report new or unusual thigh, hip, or groin pain.
Osteonecrosis of the external auditory canal has been reported with denosumab.

items.t: Skin infections (mainly cellulitis) leading to hospital admission: seek prompt care.

src.q: Patients should be advised to seek prompt medical attention if they develop signs or symptoms of cellulitis.

items.t: Do not use with other denosumab-containing products. Contains sorbitol (47 mg/mL).

src.q: Patients being treated with denosumab should not be treated concomitantly with other denosumab-containing medicinal products
This medicine contains 47 mg sorbitol in each mL of solution.

items.t: No clinically relevant pharmacokinetic interactions expected (no effect on CYP3A4 substrate midazolam). Previous alendronate did not alter denosumab.

src.q: This indicates that denosumab should not alter the pharmacokinetics of medicinal products metabolised by CYP3A4.
the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of denosumab were not altered by previous alendronate therapy

items.t: Glucocorticoids: additional risk factor for hypocalcaemia (section 4.4).

src.q: Concomitant glucocorticoid treatment is an additional risk factor for hypocalcaemia.

items.t: Other denosumab-containing products: do not combine.

src.q: Patients being treated with denosumab should not be treated concomitantly with other denosumab-containing medicinal products

items.t: No dose adjustment in renal impairment. Severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min) or dialysis: higher risk of hypocalcaemia; monitor calcium. MHRA (2014): check calcium within two weeks after the first dose in patients with risk factors such as CrCl below 30 ml/min.

src.q: No dose adjustment is required in patients with renal impairment
Patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance < 30 mL/min) or receiving dialysis are at greater risk of developing hypocalcaemia.
within two weeks after the initial dose in patients with risk factors for hypocalcaemia (eg, severe renal impairment, creatinine clearance <30 ml/min)

items.t: No data in patients on long-term systemic glucocorticoids with severe renal impairment (GFR below 30 mL/min).

src.q: No data is available in patients with long-term systemic glucocorticoid therapy and severe renal impairment (Glomerular filtration rate, GFR < 30 mL/min).

items.t: Not studied in hepatic impairment; pharmacokinetics not expected to be affected.

src.q: The safety and efficacy of denosumab have not been studied in patients with hepatic impairment
The pharmacokinetics of denosumab is not expected to be affected by hepatic impairment.

items.t: Not recommended in pregnancy or in women of child-bearing potential not using contraception. Avoid pregnancy during and for at least 5 months after treatment. Effects likely greater in the second and third trimesters.

src.q: Prolia is not recommended for use in pregnant women and women of child-bearing potential not using contraception.
Women should be advised not to become pregnant during and for at least 5 months after treatment with Prolia.

items.t: Unknown if excreted in milk; animal data suggest impaired lactation. Decide whether to stop breastfeeding or stop treatment, weighing benefits.

src.q: It is unknown whether denosumab is excreted in human milk.
A decision on whether to abstain from breast-feeding or to abstain from therapy with Prolia should be made

items.t: Women should avoid pregnancy during and for at least 5 months after treatment. No human fertility data; animal studies show no fertility harm.

src.q: Women should be advised not to become pregnant during and for at least 5 months after treatment with Prolia.
No data are available on the effect of denosumab on human fertility.

items.t: Very common: pain in extremity, musculoskeletal pain. Common: urinary tract and upper respiratory tract infection, sciatica, constipation, abdominal discomfort, rash, eczema, alopecia.

src.q: The most common side effects with denosumab (seen in more than one patient in ten) are musculoskeletal pain and pain in the extremity.
Common Common Uncommon Uncommon Uncommon Urinary tract infection Upper respiratory tract infection

items.t: Severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia (QT prolongation, tetany, seizures, altered mental state): measure calcium if symptoms occur.

src.q: Examples of the clinical manifestations of severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia have included QT interval prolongation, tetany, seizures and altered mental status
If any patient presents with suspected symptoms of hypocalcaemia during treatment (see section 4.8 for symptoms) calcium levels should be measured.

items.t: Osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fractures (rare); cellulitis (uncommon); anaphylaxis (rare). Consider stopping pending evaluation if an atypical femoral fracture is suspected.

src.q: Uncommon cases of cellulitis, rare cases of hypocalcaemia, hypersensitivity, osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fractures
Discontinuation of denosumab therapy in patients suspected to have an atypical femur fracture should be considered pending evaluation of the patient based on an individual benefit-risk assessment.

items.t: Multiple vertebral fractures after stopping or delaying treatment (MHRA).

src.q: an increased risk of multiple vertebral fractures has been reported in patients within 18 months of stopping or delaying ongoing denosumab 60mg treatment for osteoporosis

items.t: Before starting: identify hypocalcaemia risk and correct hypocalcaemia; check ONJ risk factors and arrange dental examination if present.

src.q: It is important to identify patients at risk for hypocalcaemia.
A dental examination with preventive dentistry and an individual benefit-risk assessment is recommended prior to treatment with denosumab in patients with concomitant risk factors.

items.t: Calcium before each dose; in patients predisposed to hypocalcaemia (e.g. CrCl below 30 mL/min), also within two weeks after the first dose; and whenever symptoms suggest hypocalcaemia.

src.q: Clinical monitoring of calcium levels is recommended before each dose and, in patients predisposed to hypocalcaemia within two weeks, after the initial dose.
Check calcium levels: before each dose within two weeks after the initial dose in patients with risk factors for hypocalcaemia

items.t: After stopping: monitor BMD and consider alternative treatment. Do not stop without specialist review (MHRA).

src.q: Thus, monitoring of BMD is recommended, and alternative treatment should be considered according to clinical guidelines.
patients should not stop denosumab without specialist review

items.t: Subcutaneous injection by a trained person. Let the syringe reach room temperature, do not shake, inject slowly and give the whole contents. Store refrigerated (2-8°C); may be kept at room temperature (up to 25°C) for up to 30 days.

src.q: Administration should be performed by an individual who has been adequately trained in injection techniques.
To avoid discomfort at the site of injection, allow the pre-filled syringe to reach room temperature (up to 25°C) before injecting and inject slowly.
Once removed from the refrigerator, Prolia may be stored at room temperature (up to 25°C) for up to 30 days in the original carton.

items.t: Do not stop or delay injections without talking to the doctor; if a dose is missed, have it as soon as possible.

src.q: do not stop denosumab treatment without talking to your doctor to discuss your individual risk factors

items.t: Take calcium and vitamin D as advised. Report muscle spasms, twitching, cramps or tingling (low calcium).

src.q: Tell all patients to report symptoms of hypocalcaemia to their doctor (eg, muscle spasms, twitches, or cramps; numbness or tingling in the fingers, toes, or around the mouth).

items.t: Keep good oral hygiene, have routine dental check-ups, and report loose teeth, mouth pain, swelling or non-healing sores. Report new thigh, hip or groin pain, ear symptoms, or signs of skin infection. Carry the patient reminder card.

src.q: All patients should be encouraged to maintain good oral hygiene, receive routine dental check-ups, and immediately report any oral symptoms
Patients treated with Prolia should be given the package leaflet and the patient reminder card.

Denosumab 60 mg (for osteoporosis indications) should not be used in patients with hypocalcaemia, regardless of severity
